transcript.text: Bosch built-in microwave BFL524MS0B randomly stops part way through cooking, time still on the display. Opening and closing the door lets it carry on. Maybe once every few days.

That pattern points mostly towards the door safety system. When the microwave pauses with the time still showing and then carries on as soon as you open and shut the door, it usually means the control briefly saw the door as open. This happens when a latch hook or interlock switch makes a marginal contact. Opening and closing the door resets the latch and it picks up again. Random timing, every few days, fits that kind of intermittent contact. The main alternative is the overheat protection tripping. Built-in microwaves rely on air getting in and out through the trim, so restricted ventilation can cause this. A thermal trip usually needs a cool-down before it will run again, though, rather than resuming straight away. That makes it less likely here. A loose plug or socket, or a control fault, is a distant third. Things you can safely check (switched off at the isolator or unplugged):
1. Open the door and look at the latch hooks on the door and the slots they go into. Wipe away any grease or food residue with a damp cloth, and check nothing is chipped or loose. If it then stops happening, that was the cause.
2. Close the door gently and watch whether it sits flush and clicks home fully. If it closes softly without a firm click, or sits slightly proud on one side, the door alignment or latch wear is the likely cause.
3. Make sure the vents in the trim or plinth around the microwave aren't blocked by anything stored in front of them. If it tends to stop during long cooks and feels very warm around the vents, overheating moves up the list.
4. If it's on a plug, check that the plug is pushed fully into the socket and isn't on an extension lead. If the latch area is clean and the door shuts firmly but it keeps happening, the most likely part is a door interlock (microswitch) or the latch mechanism. On a microwave, that work means going inside the casing, where high voltage can remain stored even when unplugged. That's a job for an engineer, not a DIY repair. It's worth getting it looked at, because these switches are part of the safety system. Being a built-in model, it may also need taking out of the housing. Two things would help me narrow it down. When it stops, do the light and turntable also stop? And does it seem linked to long or hot cooks, or does it happen at any point?

I cleaned some grease off the door hooks and latch slots and it still happened once since. When it stops the fan and light stop too, as if the door had been opened, and the start indicator goes off. It seems to happen more when I close the door gently, not linked to long cooks. No smell, sparks or tripping.

Your latest details pretty much settle it. When it stops, the fan and light go off and the start indicator drops out, exactly as if the door had been opened. Add that it happens more after a gentle close, it isn't linked to long cooks, and cleaning the hooks hasn't cured it, and this is the door safety circuit losing contact for a split second. It isn't overheating or a power problem. In order of likelihood:
1. A door interlock microswitch that's worn or slightly out of adjustment. It only just makes contact, so a little vibration from the fan or turntable breaks it.
2. Worn latch hooks or a slightly dropped door, so the hooks don't push the switches fully home unless the door is shut firmly.
3. Much less likely, a loose connection on the switch wiring or a control board fault. One check helps separate the first two (unplugged or isolated, door shut):
1. Gently push and pull the door edge near the handle. If there's noticeable play, or the door sits slightly proud on one side, worn hooks or alignment is more likely. If it feels solid and flush, the switch itself is the stronger suspect.
2. For the next week or so, close the door firmly every time. If the stops disappear, that suggests a marginal switch or latch rather than anything electronic. It's only a workaround, though, not a fix. Either way, the repair is the same kind of job. The interlock switches and latch sit inside the casing, where the high-voltage parts can hold a dangerous charge even when unplugged. Being built in, it also has to come out of the housing. That's one for an engineer, not DIY. The likely part is a door interlock microswitch, or the latch assembly if the hooks are worn. An engineer can test which one before fitting anything. It's usually a modest repair compared with replacing a built-in unit. If it's fairly new, check whether it's still under Bosch's guarantee or an extended warranty first, as this would normally be covered. Don't try to bypass or adjust the switches yourself. It's fine to keep using it carefully in the meantime, since it's failing safe by stopping. Stop using it straight away if the door ever seems to let it run while open or loose, or you notice sparking or burning.

Overheat protection tripping due to restricted ventilation in the built-in housing (medium)
Control/supply glitch (marginal socket or plug connection, control board) (low)
